newsitem.title: POLAND: East European ministers agree joint police actions.
newsitem.headline: East European ministers agree joint police actions.

text.p: The interior ministries of six East European states including Russia and Poland on Saturday set themselves a March 1997 target to go beyond mere talk and cooperate in getting tough against cross-border crime.

Poland's Interior Minister Zbigniew Siemiatkowski said that, for example, Moscow's undercover agents would be allowed to infiltrate close-knit Russian-speaking gangs operating in Poland, which local police have been hard-pressed to penetrate.

"We...accepted the undertaking of joint operational actions with the aim of taking really decisive and energetic action against organised crime," Siemiatkowski told reporters after a meeting of ministers and other top officials near Warsaw.

Russia's Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov and Lithuania's Virgilius Bulovas, as well as representatives of Belarus, Ukraine and Slovakia also attended and agreed to prepare a timetable of measures to be signed at a March 1 meeting.
The states have long talked about cooperation on crime, but Siemiatkowski said they would now go beyond mere declarations.

Poland aims to join the European Union within a few years and Western states have expressed concern that this may ease a westward push by crime gangs flourishing in countries of the former Soviet Union bordering Poland.
Poland has liberal arrangements for travel across its borders with Belarus, Ukraine and Lithuania and has just signed an agreement with Russia allowing visa-free travel.
This will come into effect once Warsaw and Moscow sign another pact providing for Russia to re-admit people from third countries who cross illegally from its territory into Poland.
Kulikov told reporters the mutual readmission agreement would be signed in the first quarter of 1997.
Siemiatkowski said Poland's police, cooperating with other countries, would now start applying its newly-granted legal powers to mount "sting" operations to trap criminals.

Apart from allowing foreign undercover police to function on their territories, the participating countries will also exchange intelligence on movements of known criminals and step up controls and airports and border crossings, he said.
